Le Koujina Café, le café des possibles: Koujina Café, the Café of Possibilities
À Montréal, un café tunisien devenu carr: In Montréal, a Tunisian café has become a crossroads of cultures and a symbol of integration without erasure.
Façade du café Koujina, situé sur la rue: Façade of Café Koujina, on Saint-Zotique Street, in the heart of Rosemont–La Petite-Patrie. Photo credit: Nantou Soumahoro
Qu’est-ce qui fait qu’un café de quartie: What makes a neighbourhood café become more than a café? At Koujina, I found a clue: it’s a place that doesn’t try to seduce but simply to be, and that, over time, brings people together. No folklore, no exoticism, just a simple way of putting Tunisia forward while speaking to Montréal’s cosmopolitanism. The Koujina experience raises a question: how do you showcase a culture on its own terms while welcoming a diverse population? Here, you taste flavours that transport you elsewhere while keeping you here, without pitting the two worlds against each other.
Sur la rue Saint-Zotique, au cœur de Ros: On Saint-Zotique Street, in the heart of Rosemont–La Petite-Patrie, a Tunisian café draws a diverse clientele. People push open the door for an orange blossom-scented cheesecake or an Arabic coffee. They stay for something else: a place where Tunisian cooking keeps its original flavour and where identity is fully embraced. Here, authenticity comes first. Baya and Malek, a couple in life as well as behind the counter, are betting that you can share a culture without distorting it, and integrate as an immigrant without disappearing. Having opened on October 8, 2023, Koujina Café is about to celebrate its second anniversary. A profile.
Il est 18 h, un mercredi. Des haut-parle: It’s 6 p.m. on a Wednesday. From the café’s speakers comes the voice of Ahmed Eid, singing in Arabic Balad mahjour tarkin el-qalb mazrou, which means: “An abandoned country leaves the heart rooted.” An image of nostalgia that fits the spirit of Koujina Café. “At first, we wanted to open a Tunisian-inspired café, and then, as the project developed, we really wanted to create something authentically Tunisian,” says Malek.
Pas de décor de type carte postale ni de: No postcard-style décor, no folklore for tourists. The white and blue walls recall the Mediterranean, but the intention lies elsewhere: to show a Tunisia that is self-assured, contemporary, free of clichés. Each recipe becomes a way of keeping alive here what they left behind there.
Comptoir du Café Koujina, un espace de r: The counter at Café Koujina, a space for encounters, discussion and cultural experimentation. Photo credit: Nantou Soumahoro
La carte mêle classiques et parfums tuni: The menu blends classics with Tunisian flavours: cheesecake infused with fig or geranium water, Arabic coffee, lattes made with house-made syrups. “The best known is a latte called the Mariem Latte. It’s made with condensed milk and orange blossom. It tastes very Mediterranean. You can’t find it anywhere else,” says Baya with a smile. “We wanted to evoke a Tunisia of 2025, an ultra-alive culture, adapted to today.”
À Montréal, Malek observe une autre tend: In Montréal, Malek sees another trend: “The culture of so-called ethnic restaurants is often diluted.” Baya picks up, in a rhythm that has become natural between them: “The more you dilute, the more you lose the essence. It’s important to have the real thing before you have the mix.”
Ce choix n’est pas qu’une question de go: This choice isn’t just a matter of taste, but a vision of immigration. Succeeding at integration doesn’t mean erasing your culture, argues Baya: “People often say ‘Integrate’ as if you had to cut off pieces of yourself. No. You can add as much as you want; if you start cutting back, you lose yourself.” For her, multiculturalism comes down to a simple equation: “You add, you don’t subtract.”
Ce refus de la dilution n’est pas qu’une: This refusal of dilution isn’t just about food. It comes from a broader memory, forged far from here. Because behind the cakes and coffees, there is also a political story: that of a generation shaped by the Revolution of Dignity, better known in the West as the Jasmine Revolution.
En décembre 2010, tout bascule à Sidi Bo: In December 2010, everything tips over in Sidi Bouzid. Mohamed Bouazizi, a street vendor selling fruit and vegetables, sets himself on fire after his cart is confiscated. His desperate act sets Tunisia ablaze. In January 2011, a 23-year-old regime collapses under pressure from the street. On Bourguiba Avenue in Tunis, every social class mingles, carried by the same slogans. The fall of President Ben Ali opens onto chaos: elections, a constitution, the rise and then fall of the Islamists. In this tumult, a generation is forged.
Baya et Malek font partie de cette génér: Baya and Malek are part of that generation. Teenagers at the time, they discovered politics in the street, amid the slogans and the clashes. “We removed a dictator, we put in a democracy. The Muslim Brotherhood came in, then we kicked out the Muslim Brotherhood. In short, a thousand and one things happened,” Malek sums up. In his memory, the city was beheading itself in order to rebuild better. Everything became political, even conversations on the street.
Baya, alors une collégienne de 12 ans, g: Baya, then a 12-year-old middle schooler, remembers the image of Kasbah Square. She watched the crowd from a street above. “A lot was happening there,” she says quietly. What she saw, she has never forgotten: bodies clashing, people from everywhere fighting over opinions. “I saw people sew their mouths shut, really wild things. But it was for ideas.” Not a war over territory or money: a fight for convictions.
De cette époque, ils gardent le souvenir: From that time, they keep the memory of an irresistible momentum. “It broke down the barriers between classes a bit,” Malek points out. “In the end, we’re a generation where everybody talked to each other.” Even those who didn’t live through the revolution directly, he adds, “are even more revolutionary than we are, without knowing it.” For Baya, that energy left a lasting mark: “It sinks in. It’s the idea that everything is possible.”

Pour Malek, un piège guette trop souvent: For Malek, there is a trap that too often lies in wait for stories of identity: victimhood. The weight of colonization and wars is undeniable, he acknowledges, but he refuses to reduce an entire culture to it. “A lot of people I meet tell me, ‘Twenty years ago, there was war [in Tunisia].’ Yes. But twenty years ago, there was also singing. Forty years ago, there was also music.”
Son insistance met en lumière une volont: His insistence highlights a desire not to be defined solely by pain. “Yes, there were people who took, who stole. But despite that, we kept creating, kept developing.” For him, recent generations are taking up the torch of unfinished battles and pushing further: “We’re among the great doctors, the great thinkers. We have the capacity to build something new, more suited, more functional,” adds Baya. “Now it’s up to us too to really put in the effort needed to rebuild what was unfortunately deconstructed, broken.”
Cette vision des choses trouve à se trad: This outlook finds expression in Koujina Café, which has become a testing ground: DJ sets, comedy nights, board game tournaments, a film club. And there’s no question of sliding into misery-centred portrayals: “For the first screening, we showed Porto Farina,” Baya recalls. Ibrahim Letaief’s joyful, colourful film contrasts with the image usually pinned on North Africa, which dwells on sadness, war and famine. In a space where barely 45 chairs can be set up on screening nights, the idea is to offer an intimate experience. Audience members are close to one another, and sometimes to the filmmakers too, with whom they can then talk. “Here, it’s 50% film, 50% discussion,” Baya adds with a smile.
La même logique traverse l’organisation: The same logic runs through the café’s details: a display built into one of the walls offers 100% Tunisian products for sale. “We wanted to show that in Tunisia, there’s art direction, brands that compete with imports. We buy Tunisian not out of patriotism, but because it’s good and well made.”
Plus loin, dans la salle, près d’un cana: Farther along, in the room, near a couch, vinyl records and books by Tunisian artists sit enthroned on a piece of furniture. The idea is always the same: lay out Tunisian culture, make it accessible, without turning it into a curiosity.
Et derrière tout cela, une méthode : gra: And behind all of this, a method: scratch. “Scratch at your culture. Talk to people. A large part of our stories has been erased, sometimes intentionally. Not everything has been written down.” Malek says that to those who want to visit Tunisia, he advises seeing the tourist sites, but above all talking to people. “People will take you where no one else has access.”
Pour eux, c’est une responsabilité de gé: For them, it’s a generational responsibility: completing a fragmented memory. “History was written by the colonizers. Today, we have the right to rewrite it.” And the internet, adds Baya, lets us go faster: “It’s up to us to push out every truth, even the ones that are disturbing and uncomfortable. Whether it’s your grandmother’s story or your neighbour’s, it’s all part of your story.”
Leur démarche ne s’arrête pas aux fronti: Their approach doesn’t stop at Tunisia’s borders: it aims to give every culture the chance to be seen in its vitality and joy.

Au café, Malek et Baya multiplient les o: At the café, Malek and Baya create one opportunity after another to mix communities: a Tunisian-Senegalese DJ set, an evening devoted to Lebanon, another to Palestine. The reactions speak for themselves: Syrians surprised to hear the songs of their childhood, Senegalese moved to see their culture shown in a way other than through misery, Palestinians happy to associate their country with celebration rather than bombings. “Here, it’s music, song, food, in short, a living culture,” Baya says happily.

Et la liste s’allonge : « On a eu aussi: And the list keeps growing: “We’ve also had Israelis, Ukrainians, Chinese, Japanese…” Malek lists. At these evenings, languages intertwine, rhythms answer one another and stories circulate over a cup of coffee. Every time, the surprise is the same: seeing yourself represented in a way other than through tragedy. “All cultures are good, all ways of living are good. What matters is to embrace them and live fully with them,” Baya concludes.
Les commentaires des clients confirment: Customers’ comments confirm this idea. One evening, a group of Ukrainians came to tell them: “Your relationship with your culture helps us present ourselves differently in relation to our own.” Listening to a Ukrainian song thus becomes a normal act that has nothing patriotic about it and is explained simply by the fact that it’s a good song.
Le Koujina Café n’est pas un sanctuaire,: Koujina Café is not a sanctuary but a kitchen, which is exactly what the name means! “The kitchen is where we talk frankly, where the gossip, the music, the smells pass through,” Malek smiles. An everyday, living place where ideas circulate, collide, are debated.
Pour eux, le café doit rester un échanti: For them, the café should remain a sample of a world where coexistence is possible on one condition: respecting three simple rules. “Don’t mistreat anyone, don’t disrespect anyone and let everyone live as they want.”
Et parfois, cette cohabitation donne à v: And sometimes, this coexistence produces unexpected scenes. “We’ve had North African LGBTQ+ people and people who don’t accept diverse gender identities sitting at neighbouring tables,” says Malek. In that kind of situation, there are two options: confront each other or drink your coffee in peace. “It’s always the second one that wins out.”
La mission du café n’est pas d’éduquer o: The café’s mission isn’t to educate Montrealers or explain Tunisia to them, but to show it to them as it is. “We don’t tell anyone how to think. We set the context, we listen. And we accept contradiction,” Malek insists.
Le concept du Koujina Café n’a pas été é: The concept for Koujina Café wasn’t developed as part of a business plan, but out of a deliberate kind of carefreeness. “Nobody told us, ‘Go for it, it’s a good idea,’” Malek confides. “Apart from a few loved ones who supported us, everyone else kept saying: at 25, you should finish school, think before jumping in!”
Chaque rendez-vous à la banque faisait r: Every meeting at the bank brought up the same doubts. “Do you know how to do this?” the banker would ask. “No, but if I say I’m going to do it, I learn and I do it,” Malek would answer. A sincerity that, paradoxically, helped them, because nothing in reality destined them for the restaurant business. Malek studied psychology, and Baya political science and public relations. “It let us use our knowledge a bit to get a perspective other than just business or restaurants. It’s good to cross disciplines,” says Baya. She hadn’t gone to pastry school either, but she was already creating. “I design cakes, I taste, I have others taste. I don’t have a recipe book. It’s a lot of trial and error. It’s fun.”
Le café s’est construit comme ses recett: The café was built like its recipes: through trial and error, discussion and improvisation. At 26, they opened without a safety net, despite the warnings. They gave up everything: the daily grind that bored them, their stable jobs. “Now, it’s an adventure!” Baya goes on. An adventure in all its harshness and joy: fingers smelling of sugar and coffee, short nights, long mornings, but also a new kind of freedom. “It’s this carefreeness that saved us,” Malek continues. “We didn’t wait to have all the answers. We just did it.”
Mais le parcours n’a pas été simple. À 2: But the road hasn’t been easy. Now 28, they smile as they think back on their beginnings. “Opening a café with no experience is really hard. And on top of that, we had no money,” Baya remembers. “We put in everything we had, and even what we didn’t have.” For the first eight months, they couldn’t hire anyone. “We were our own employees,” Malek reports with amusement. Twelve, 14, 16 hours a day, sometimes 20 in a row: “You had to get dirty, come home late, wake up early, stop seeing your friends.”
Avec le recul, ils le reconnaissent : c’: Looking back, they acknowledge it: it was their mindset that made the adventure possible. “We had an attitude: if we don’t know, we learn, and we do,” says Malek. Their tenacity, they say, also comes from what Tunisia passed on to them through its struggles.
Au moment de célébrer le deuxième annive: As they celebrate their café’s second anniversary, Baya and Malek can be glad that Koujina’s energy hasn’t waned. The two owners keep experimenting, listening to cravings, testing combinations: lemon-basil cheesecake, date syrup latte, walnut cake.
Avec le temps, cette souplesse a fini pa: Over time, this flexibility has ended up creating much more than a clientele: a community. “We didn’t manufacture this community, it happened at the counter,” Malek observes. Regulars no longer come only for a coffee, but for the bond woven with the place and its owners. “If someone comes three times, naturally I ask them, ‘How are you? What’s going on in your life?’” Little by little, faces repeat, stories intertwine and the place becomes a witness. “We’ve seen customers get pregnant and come back with their baby,” Baya smiles. The café’s rhythms are also shaped by the rhythms of its customers’ lives. One night during Ramadan, at 11 p.m., the room was still full. An employee from the neighbouring bar, intrigued, knocked on the window: “Why are you packed?” he asked in astonishment. “Because it’s Ramadan,” Malek replied. “Because we opened at night. Because a café can hold two rhythms at once: that of the neighbourhood and that of a moveable feast.”
Cette ouverture et l’esprit du lieu atti: This openness and the spirit of the place attract a loyal clientele, ready to cross the city to get there. Jamila, a student of Algerian origin, comes once a week or every two weeks, despite a half-hour trip from Côte-des-Neiges: “The atmosphere is really beautiful, I like studying here. The menu is unique, it suits my tastes. And it brings me back to a North African culture, with a touch of modernity that’s a pleasure.”
Aaron, lui, a découvert l’endroit grâce: Aaron discovered the place through his girlfriend: “It’s a one-of-a-kind café. The décor and the menu both feel good. I tried a Mariem Latte, it’s one of the best I’ve had. I’ll be back, for sure.”
